a vigorous vegetative cover which provides wildlife ha bitat and erosion control.  Following six- or eight-
years’ growth, biomass can be harvested for a variet y of forest product usages including mulch, fuel, 
pulp/paper feedstock, compost bulking agent, and as a bioenergy fuel source. 
 
Researchers from the University of Maryland conducted a multi-year field study evaluating the application 
of biosolids using the Deep Row Entrenchment (DRE) method in hybrid poplar plantations. Biosolids were 
applied in subsurface trenches at rates up to 294 dry tons per acre and covered with soil to promote 
nutrient uptake while minimizing environmental exposure. The study focused on nutrient dynamics—
particularly nitrogen and phosphorus—and employed a comprehensive monitoring system including 
suction lysimeters and twelve groundwater wells inst alled at varying depths and locations. These wells 
tracked nutrient migration throughout the study period under different biosolid application rates and soil 
conditions. 
 
Phosphorus, like nitrogen, played a critical role in supporting tree growth. The hybrid poplars maintained 
foliar phosphorus concentrations within the optimal range (0.25–0.40%), indicating sufficient uptake for 
fast growth and biomass development. Phosphorus supplied in biosolids was present in both organic and 
inorganic forms, with organic P slowly mineralizing over time to match tree demand. Due to phosphorus’s 
strong tendency to bind with iron and aluminum oxides in soil, its availability to plants was steady but not 
excessive, and vertical mobility was inherently low. Cycling occurred primarily within the root zone, where 
microbial activity and tree uptake helped retain  P near the trenches. Importantly, groundwater 
monitoring data showed no measurable increases in phosphorus concentrations over time, and 
monitoring wells downgradient from high-rate applications remained consistent with background levels. 
 
The study also found no evidence of phosphorus movement via surface runoff, which is often a greater 
risk than leaching in typical agri cultural applications. Because the biosolids were deeply buried and 
covered with overburden soil, the system effectively prevented direct surface exposure and erosion. This 
method of application eliminates key pathways for environmental loss, including volatilization, runoff, 
and vector contact. Overall, the deep row entrenchment system proved highly effective in containing and 
cycling phosphorus in a controlled root environment.  Combined with low nitrate leaching, robust tree 
uptake, and no adverse water quality impacts, the findings support the conclusion that biosolids applied 
through this method do not pose a threat to human health or the environment. 
 
The University of Maryland (UMD) fact sheet entitled, “ Use of Deep Row Biosolids Applications to Grow 
Forest Trees” provides a broad overview of the technique.  In summary, this method involves excavation 
of shallow trenches.  Biosolids received at the site are placed in the trench to approximately 2/3 of the 
cut depth and then promptly covered with excavated soil.  Rows are typically placed on eight-foot centers.  
Thus, using this strategy, a one-acre parcel will contain approximately 5,400 lineal feet of shallow trench 
rows.  Overburden from the excavation of one row is placed as cover on the adjacent biosolids-filled row.  
Prior to planting, a bulldozer is used to level the ov erburden so  that it consistently covers entrenched 
biosolids.  Poplar tree sticklings are typically planted on a 10-foot grid pattern, but other spaces have been 
used. 
 
The biosolids loading rate for the WN site will be  calculated using the QEG Tree Farm nutrient 
management tool (TFN

on the TFNMT. The individual trench at WN will be up to 60 inches wide and 20 to 49 inches deep, installed 
on 8-foot centers (assuming 74 lb. per cubic foot biosolids density).  The maximum proposed trench 
excavation depth is therefore set at 49 inches.  Previous deep row biosolids studies have used loading 
rates as high as 517 dry tons per acre and found that poplars cultivated on sites employing even these 
high loading rates can experience plant tissue N and phosphorus (P) deficiencies.  Poplars are known to 
immobilize as much as 500 lbs. N per acre per year (M urray 2003, as cited by Buswell, 2006).  Even with 
these high N uptake rates, it is clear that a very la rge fraction of the biosolids N is being denitrified (as 
nitrogen gas lost to the atmosphere).  Hence, conventional plant available nitrogen (PAN) factors 
commonly used for surface-applied (or shallow-tilled) biosolids do not apply for deep row recycling. 
 
Nitrogen movement into sub-surface waters was studie d at Virginia Polytechnic Institute from 2006 to 
2010 through USDA Reels grants in Sussex County at the Iluka mining site.  In this study coarse (sandy) 
soils were the local soils and study basis.  In this situation it was noted that N will leach and that very 
coarse soils are not suitable for trenching. Fortunately, the WN site has predominantly clay soils to deter 
N and P losses of concern.   
 
Poplars are an ideal species for deep row plantations as these trees develop extensive rooting systems to 
60 inches depth, tolerate waterlogged and drought conditions, exhibit high survival rates, and have very 
high water uptake and evapotranspiration rates.  Poplar clone OP367 has been identified as the best 
species for deep row recycling, showing the highest survival rate and best growth characteristics in studies 
performed by UMB researchers (UMB, Fact Sheet entitled Five-year Study Results for Hybrid Poplar Clone 
Study by Using Deep Row Biosolids Incorporation and will be used exclusively for this project.  Interestingly, 
hybrid poplar plantings have been used in riparian buffer research to reduce soil profile and near-surface 
groundwater nitrate concentrations in excess of 90 mg/L to 2 mg/L (Licht 1990, as cited by Buswell, 2006).  
There is potential for further research into using various species of trees for biosolids tree farms based on 
researcher recommendations and preferences and will be done by Dr. Nick Basta, Soil Scientist from Ohio 
State University. 
 
Deep row biosolids recycling employs very high total N loading rates, which at first seem difficult to 
reconcile with respect to crop uptake.  Success of the deep row system hinges on delayed biological 
decomposition resulting from anoxic conditions created by trenching a layer of biosolids.  Cool subsurface 
temperatures also have a significant impact on microbiological activity.  Pepperman (1995, as cited by 
Evanylo, 2008) found that over a six-year hybrid poplar rotation, 12,000 lbs. or biosolids N per acres was 
insufficient to provide adequate plant tissue N content.  Investigators estimated that 40 percent of 
biosolids N was denitrified and lost to the atmosphere .  After six to nine years, poplar tissue N content 
dropped below 3.5 percent, signaling N deficiency.  Pepperman found that entrenching biosolids resulted 
in very slow generation of nitrate (an aerobic process), and the subsequent denitrification (anoxic process) 
of any nitrate-N that is not quickly assimilated by tree roots.

coarse textured soil.  Mineralization of organic N is diminished and nitrification of ammonium to nitrate 
is retarded in the buried material.  The oxygen de ficient environment also decreases nitrate leaching 
through denitrification.  As poplar roots penetrate the biosolids layer, oxygen is introduced (via specialized 
poplar root physiology) and nitrification begins.  As  nitrate is generated, poplar plant roots uptake the 
nutrient before it has an opportunity to leach.  Thus, it is essential that the bottom of the entrenched 
biosolids be maintained shallow enough (from soil surf ace) for poplar roots to completely surround and 
penetrate the buried material.  As shown in Figure 2, typical finished trench construction dimensions 
provide ample opportunity for poplar root encirclement and penetration, well within the 60-inch rooting 
depth capability.

not increase (a secondary indicator of water contact with biosolids).  This investigation concluded that

5.0 LAND APPLICATION 
 
This section of the LAMP is included to provide additional supporting information for Supplement to Ohio 
EPA PTI Form A-C1, sections C1 through C10. 
 
For specifics on tree planting, irrigation, growth/health monitoring, survivability, weed and damage 
control, replacement protocols, and soil and foliar sampling, please see the following Standard Operating 
Procedures (SOPs) that have been submitted to Ohio EPA through the trade secret process.

5.1 Biosolids Staging and Land Application 
 
Biosolids will be hauled to the WN from genera ting NPDES permitted POTWs and/or other NPDES 
permitted anaerobic digestion facilities by truck with ta rp.  Biosolids will be off-loaded and field stored.  
Per OAC 3745-40-07, biosolids will meet isolation distance requirements, VA R requirements, and be 
stored for up to 7 days.  From staging, biosolids will be loaded onto an off-road vehicle for hauling to the 
WN trench sites or pushed into trenches at proper loading rates. Biosolids will be off-loaded adjacent to, 
or directly into excavated trenches and promptly covered with overburden. Biosolids will be trenched up 
to 49” from the surface and covered with up to 20” overburden. The ideal amount of overburden is 12”-
20”, but still being evaluated. The staging areas will be carefully considered, isolated from population 
centers, and will meet all requirements in OAC 3745-40. The staging areas will be carefully considered and 
is isolated from population centers. Trenching, loading, and covering details can be found in the separately 
submitted SOP’s. 
 
5.2 Loading Rate Calculations 
 
As described in detail below, application rates will be determined using the QEG TFNMT.  The unique 
aspect of this project in terms of growing trees with  biosolids as a source of nutrients, is that the 
agronomic rate is based on crop nitrogen need for multiple years until the crop is harvested and on the 
expected loss of N to the atmosphere due to anoxic conditions.  Hybrid poplar trees can readily utilize 500 
lbs. of N per acre each year.  Crop rotation is typica lly six to eight years for the hybrid poplar cultivation 
in deep-row biosolids recycling operations.  Mean standing wood biomass of hybrid poplar crops grown 
in deep-row systems after six years has been reported at approximately 19,720 lbs. per acre (dry weight), 
or 9.9 tons per acre (equivalent to 45.2 lbs. per tree biomass production). 
 
Calculation of an N-based agronomic rate for deep-row recycling is problematic because of the cool, moist, 
anoxic conditions created by trenching organic material containing about 80% moisture.  These conditions 
are not typically considered in the biosolids minerali zation factors recognized by regulatory agencies.  
Deep row technology has been subjected to disciplined study in recent years.  Felton et al. (2008) have

studied application rates of 172 DTPA (16,000 lbs. total N per acre); 345 DTPA (32,000 lbs. total N per 
acre), and 517 DTPA (48,000 lbs. total N per acre) and concluded the following: 
 
1) “For the first three years (following installation), zero nitrate left the deep row tree system.” 
2) “Ammonium was immediately released into the soil surrounding the biosolids.” 
3) “Ammonium concentrations decreased dramatically with distance from the biosolids, falling from 
2,100 mg N/L at 15 cm (6 inches) from the biosolids to 400 mg N/L at 60 cm (24 inches) from the 
biosolids.” 
4) “Overall, nitrate concentrations are lower than those found beneath corn crops while utilizing a 
great deal higher application of nitrogen.” 
 
The 32,000 pounds of nitrogen per acre cited in the Felton & Kays (2014) study represents the total 
nitrogen applied through high-rate biosolid incorporation using the deep row entrenchment (DRE) 
method. In this treatment, biosolids were applied at a rate of 294 dry tons per acre, which equates to 
588,000 pounds of material per acre. Based on typical municipal biosolid nitrogen concentrations—
around 5.5% by dry weight—this translates to approximately 32,150 pounds of total nitrogen per acre. 
This value reflects the full nitrogen mass added to the system, not just the portion immediately available 
to plants or subject to leaching. The purpose of usi ng this high application rate was to evaluate nutrient 
retention, uptake by hybrid poplar trees, and the potential for nitrogen migration through the soil profile. 
The study found that despite this substantial nitrogen load, nitrate levels in the soil and groundwater 
remained within safe limits, underscoring the effectiveness of deep row entrenchment in containing 
nutrients and supporting long-term tree growth without posing a risk to water quality. 
Instead of basing application rates solely on the bi osolids weight, a calculator has been developed using 
guidance from the USEPA Biosolids Management Handbook  and independent research studies on 
application rates for biosolids tree farms.  Application rates of any particular biosolids will determine the 
appropriate trench depth (up to 49 inches) for incorporation.  The target nitrogen rate is 32,150 lbs. (total 
N) per acre.  Subsequent surface application of liquid biosolids may be needed to provide enough nitrogen 
for the crops.  This will be determined through soil and foliar testing for potential nitrogen deficiency. 
 
Phosphorous loading rates are calculated to be approximately 55 pounds of P2O5 per tree, based on a 
stand of 600 trees per acre. This data is based on  the average dry units from the primary tree farm 
generator (18% Total Solids, 40,000 mg/kg Dry Total P). Because most of this P is bound and insoluble, 
excess P must be applied to provide each tree with what is necessary for growth. Additionally, lowering 
the P application rate would also lower the Nitrogen application, thus starving the tree and killing it. 
Generators with higher N to P ratios would provide lower P loading rates.

Biosolids generated at each POTW proposed for bene ficial use in Appendix B will be monitored by the 
biosolids generator as required by Ohio EPA.  Anal ytical information per each generator’s NPDES will be 
kept on file for verification that biosolids meet Class B requirements.

Soils in the land application areas have been invest igated using the NRCS/USDA web soil survey, as well 
as a recent investigation by a soil scientist. Resear ch consistently shows that deep row entrenchment 
(DRE) of biosolids in hybrid poplar plantations is a safe and effective method for nutrient recycling with 
minimal environmental risk. Multiple field studies in Maryland and Pennsylvania have demonstrated that

Phosphorus from biosolids played a critical role in  sustaining poplar growth while remaining largely 
immobile in the soil profile. The phosphorus was gradually mineralized and taken up by tree roots, aided 
by strong sorption to iron and aluminum oxides, and retained in the root zone by microbial activity and 
perennial vegetation cover. Studies also suggest ad ded benefits of biosolids in alkaline soils, where 
phosphorus and iron deficiencies often limit growth—applications improved both nutrient availability and 
tree health without leading to heavy metal accumulation  or surface runoff (Brown et al., 2011). Parallel 
research in hybrid poplar phytoremediation system s irrigated with nutrient-rich wastewater supports 
these findings: nutrient losses—particularly for nitrate—were minimal, and nutrient retention within the 
plant-soil system was high (Guidi et al., 2010). Even  in fertilized, short-rotation coppice systems, nitrate 
loss to the environment tends to decline over time due to aggressive root uptake and permanent ground 
cover (Well et al., 2016). Collectively, these studies confirm that biosolids, when used in deep-row systems 
with fast-growing trees, pose minimal risk to human health or the environment while delivering long-term 
agronomic and ecological benefits.  We form ally request a Director’s waiver from the 
phosphorus/nitrogen agronomic rated limitations in OAC 3745-40 for this project. 
 
5.4 Weather Conditions 
 
All biosolids will be staged on location.  Once it is moved to the WN trenching operation, it will be 
incorporated (placed in an excavated trench and covered with overburden/soil) during operations.  
Biosolids can and will be land-applied throughout the year.  Biosolids can be stored on site up to 7 days 
before being placed in trenches and covered with overburden.  However, if it is raining or greater than 0.5 
inches of rain is in the 24-hour forecast, biosolids will be placed in trenches and covered with overburden 
the same day as delivery.  If for any reason this ca nnot be accomplished, filter socks will be used to 
surround stored piles in the field.

5.6 Frozen/Snow Covered Ground 
 
If the ground is snow-covered when the biosolids are delivered, the unloading area will be cleared of snow, 
the biosolids will be unloaded, placed in trenches and covered with overburden the same day as delivery.  
If the ground can be excavated, it is not defined as frozen ground.  If the ground is frozen and therefore, 
cannot be excavated, biosolids will not be delivered to the site until the ground can be excavated (and 
therefore not frozen). 
 
 
 
 
5.7 Odor/Nuisance Management 
 
Field staging areas will be located > 100 feet from the nearest roadside ditch.  Same day covering of 
biosolids will assist in minimizing odors and establishment of quick-growing mixed grass vegetative cover 
(between the rows, if needed) will minimize erosion on areas where trenches have been filled and graded.

Please see the enclosed maps attached to this Land Application Management Plan.  Map 1 shows the 
general project site location and the setbacks.  Additional maps are provided in the Soil and Site Evaluation 
Report in Appendix C. 
6.0 ENVIRONMENTAL MONITORING 
 
6.1 Ground Water/Surface Water 
 
No impacts to ground water or surface water are anticipated.  See Soil and Site Evaluation Report in 
Appendix C for ground water and surface water site conditions.  Ground water monitoring is planned and 
the plan shall be submitted to Ohio EPA upon approval of this LAMP.  The plan will be developed in 
accordance with OAC 3745-42-13. 
 
Surface flow of water on the site is primarily to the pond in the northeast corner of the site.  The pond has 
an outlet to the north, so surface water monitoring w ill be conducted.  Prior to biosolids arriving on the 
site, a baseline monitoring sample will be collected from near the northern pond outlet.  The sample will 
be analyzed for pH, specific conductivity, nitrate-N, nitrite-N, ammonium-N, chloride, sulfate, and total 
phosphorus.  A baseline monitoring report with the results will be submitted to Ohio EPA prior to biosolids 
arriving on site.  Once biosolid trenching operations begin, quarterly surface water sampling at the same 
location as the baseline sampling will be conducted.  The quarterly samples will be analyzed for the same 
parameters as the baseline sample.

text:
Soil and Site Evaluation  2065 Rombach Avenue 
Quasar Energy Group – Wilmington Nursery  Wilmington, Ohio 44177 
 
   
ENVi Environmental, LLC                                                                      - 3 - Elyria, Ohio 
 
1.0 PROJECT OVERVIEW 
  
The Wilmington Nursery (WN) site is an agricultural property located in Wilmington, Clinton County, Ohio.  
WN will beneficially use Class B Biosolids to aid the growth of harvestable trees to be processed into mulch 
or bioenergy.  ENVi Environmental, LLC (ENVi) prep ared this Soil and Site Evaluation (SSE) has been 
prepared to support the GrowNow LLC (GrowNow) Permit-to-Install (PTI) application and Land Application 
Management Plan (LAMP) for land application of biosolids at the WN site.   
 
The WN site is approximately 138 acres of agricultural land located at 2065 Rombach Avenue, in 
Wilmington, Clinton County, Ohio.  A site map and a USGS topographic map are included as Figures 1 and 
2.  A man-made pond and its banks cover approximately 26 acres of the site.  Shallow drainage swales are 
present on the central portion of the site.  One of these extends northeast across the site to the pond and 
the other is located extends east along the north-central property boundary.  No water was present in 
these swales during the site evaluation field work in May 2025.  A farmhouse and four grain silos are 
located on the southwest portion of the site.  Agricultur al fields that were fallow at the time of the site 
evaluation field work, cover the remainder of the site.   
 
On May 15 and 16, 2025, under the supervision of ENVi personnel, 12 soil borings (B1 through B12) were 
advanced at the site.  Soil borings were advanced to terminal depths ranging from 12 to 31 feet below 
ground surface (bgs) using a track-mounted direct pu sh drill rig.  Drilling services were performed by 
Envirocore, Inc. of Plain City, Ohio.  The soil borings were logged by Ann M. Winegar, PG, a licensed 
Professional Geologist, using the Unified Soil Classification System (USCS).  The boring logs are included in 
Appendix A. 
 
In conjunction with the logging by the geologist, a Certified Professional Soil Scientist (CPSS) described 
and logged the soil from test holes that were hand augered next to the direct push boring locations.  Jeff 
Rice, CPSS with ABC Soil, LLC, performed the soil sc ientist services.  The test holes were augered to 
terminal depths ranging from 60 to 70 inches bgs and each test hole identification number corresponds 
to the boring identification number (for example, test hole #1 corresponds to boring B1).   The soil scientist 
soil descriptions are provided on the Soil Descriptions for On-Site Sewage Treatment Systems forms and 
are included in Appendix B. 
2.0 MAP AND GEOLOGICAL RESOURCE REVIEW 
 
2.1 Wetlands  
 
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) National Wetlands Inventory (NWI) Map from the NWI online 
mapper shows two ponds located approximately 200 feet south of the site.  The ponds are man-made and 
are classified as PUBGx (Palustrine, Unconsolidated Bottom, Intermittently Exposed, Excavated).  Two 
intermittent streams are shown near the site. One of these is located near the southeast corner of the 
site and flows from one of the ponds south of the site and the other is located approximately 900 feet 
west of the site.  Both are classified as R4SBC (Riverine, Intermittent, Streambed, Seasonally Flooded).  A 
copy of the NWI map is included in Appendix C.

title: 1MP00060.pdf
text:
Soil and Site Evaluation  2065 Rombach Avenue 
Quasar Energy Group – Wilmington Nursery  Wilmington, Ohio 44177 
 
   
ENVi Environmental, LLC                                                                      - 4 - Elyria, Ohio 
 
2.2 Topography and Physiographic Region 
 
According to the Ohio Department of Natural Resources publication, Physiographic Regions of Ohio, the 
site is located within the Southern Ohio Loamy Till Plai n.  The publication indicates that this till plain is 
characterized by having a surface of loamy till, end and recessional moraines, commonly associated with 
boulder belts, between relatively flat-lying ground moraine.  The United States Geological Survey (USGS) 
7.5 Minute Topographic Map of the Wilmington, Ohio Quadrangle, shows that the regional topography 
reflects this with upland areas where end or recessional moraines are present and separated by lower, 
flatter ground moraine deposits.   
 
The southwest corner of the site is located on a topographic high with the ground surface sloping down 
to the north and east.  The ground surface elevation of the site ranges from approximately 1,090 feet 
above mean sea level (amsl) at the southwest corner of the site, down to approximately 1,042 feet amsl 
on the southeast corner of the site.  The ground surface on the banks of the pond located on the northeast 
corner of the site is approximately 1,048 feet amsl.  The topographic elevations of the site are shown on 
the Soil Evaluation Map included in Appendix B. 
 
2.3 Surficial and Bedrock Geology 
 
According to the ODNR Division of Geological Survey, Ohio Geology Interactive Map, the surficial material 
on the west half of the site (where the elevations are higher) is glacial end moraine deposits and on the 
lower, flatter east half of the site is ground moraine.   The thickness of these deposits (over bedrock) is 
shown as ranging from 31 to 60 feet on the east side of the site and 61 to 100 feet on the west side of the 
site.  The uppermost bedrock is shown as dolomite and shale formations (Cedarville Dolomite, Springfield 
Dolomite, Euphemia Dolomite, Massie Shale, and Laurel Dolomite, undivided).   
 
The ODNR Division of Geological Survey publications, Quaternary Geology of Clinton County, Ohio, (Nash, 
2020) and Glacial Geology of Clinton County, Ohio  (Teller, 1967), indicate that Caesar Till End Moraine 
covers the west half of the site and the Caesar Till Ground Moraine covers the east half of the site.  The 
end moraine is associated with the regional, Wilmin gton End Moraine and the crest of this end moraine 
forms the topographic high on the west side of the site.  The Caesar Till is described as a silt loam, blue-
gray, pebbly diamicton that is typically capped with 40 to 60 inches of loess cover.  It is associated with 
the Fincastle, Reesville, Treaty, and Xenia soils in Clinton County.  The dominant pebble lithologies are 
dolomite and limestone with minor proportions of igneaous/metamorphic and shale/sandstone lithic 
fragments.  Bedrock topography shown on the Glacial Geology of Clinton County, Ohio (Teller, 1967) map 
indicates that bedrock is typically 65 to 85 feet bgs. 
 
2.4 Groundwater 
 
The Ohio Geology Interactive Map shows that the primary aquifer beneath the site is limestone and shale 
with groundwater yields that range from 3 to 10 gallons per minute (gpm) and 10 to 25 gpm.  The 
publication, Ground Water Pollution Potential of Clinton County, Ohio , (Schmidt, 1995) describes the 
hydrogeologic setting where the site is located as: 
 
“This hydrogeologic setting is characterized by low relief with limestone or dolomite bedrock 
covered by varying thicknesses of glacial till.  The till is composed of clay, silt, sand, and gravel.

title: 1MP00060.pdf
text:
Soil and Site Evaluation  2065 Rombach Avenue 
Quasar Energy Group – Wilmington Nursery  Wilmington, Ohio 44177 
 
   
ENVi Environmental, LLC                                                                      - 5 - Elyria, Ohio 
 
Sand and gravel deposits within the till are gene rally not sufficiently thick to develop as a water 
supply.  The limestone-dolomite bedrock serves as the aquifer in this setting.  Ground water 
occurs in the fractured and solutioned portions of the formation.  Recharge for the bedrock is 
from precipitation infiltration through the glacial t ill.  Depth to water is highly variable, based in 
part on the thickness of glacial sediments. Soils are typically clay loam.” 
 
The publication indicates that the hydrogeologic setting where the site is located has groundwater 
pollution potential indexes ranging from 96 to 128.  This falls within the middle portion of the index scale 
indicating that groundwater in the area has a moderate vulnerability for pollution.   
 
The ODNR Division of Geological Survey Water Well Locator shows the closest groundwater well to the 
site is located approximately 1,070 feet south of the west side of the site.  Seven documented water wells 
are located within 1,500 feet of the site.  A copy of the Water Well Location Map and the logs for these 
wells are included in Appendix D. 
 
Two groundwater monitoring wells and one injection (for shallow groundwater treatment) are located at 
a gas station site approximately 1,450 feet south of the site, along Rombach Avenue.  These wells were 
drilled to terminal depths ranging from 12.3 to 16 feet bgs and static water levels were reported at 4 to 6 
feet bgs.  The well logs indicate a general subsurface  profile of interbedded silt, sand, clay, and gravel.  
The ODNR Water Well Locator indicates that these three wells were sealed.   
 
The other six groundwater wells located within 1,500 feet of the site were drilled to terminal depths 
ranging from 51 to 90 feet bgs.  The well logs indi cate a general subsurface profile of primarily clay, 
underlain by limestone and shale bedrock.  Bedrock was reported as first encountered at depths ranging 
from 40 to 76 feet bgs.  Static water levels were reported at depths ranging from 11 to 85 feet bgs.   
 
The Ohio EPA Sole Source Aquifer map indicates that the closest sole source aquifer is over 10 miles from 
the site and the Ohio EPA Drinking Water Source Protection Area map indicates that the closest 
groundwater public water system is located over 6 miles from the site.  According to the City of 
Wilmington, Ohio website, the source for the City of  Wilmington public water supply (which serves the 
area of the site) is Caesar Creek Lake, located approximately 12 miles northwest of the site.   
 
2.5 Karst 
 
Karst terrains occur where carbonate bedrock (limestone and dolomite) is eroded by groundwater 
through dissolution.  The ODNR Division of Geological Survey publication 2024 Karst Annual Report, Karst 
Mapping of Warren and Clinton Counties, Ohio, indicates that karst features are found in areas of central 
and western Ohio where glacial deposits are thinner than about 25 feet.  The map of the study area (which 
included all of Clinton County) shows the nearest kars t feature identified was over 5 miles southwest of 
the site, where glacial deposits were thinner than 25 feet.  Karst features at the WN site are unlikely as 
glacial deposits around the site are typically much thicker than 25 feet.  The glacial deposits around the 
WN site range from 65 to 85 feet according to geological publications (see Section 2.3) and average 
thickness of 47 feet based on reviewed ODNR well logs (see Section 2.4).

text:

Quasar Energy Group – Wilmington Nursery  Wilmington, Ohio 44177 
 
   
ENVi Environmental, LLC                                                                      - 6 - Elyria, Ohio 
 
2.6 Soil Survey 
 
The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) Web Soil Survey 
shows that site is primarily covered by Fincastle silt loam, Treaty silty clay loam, and Xenia silt loam soil 
units.  Approximately 2.7% of the site is covered by Russell-Xenia silt loams (on the northwest portion of 
the site) and approximately 0.2% is covered by Sloan silt loam (southeast corner of the site).  The Soil Map 
from the Web Soil Survey is included in Appendix E. 
 
2.7 Flood Hazard 
 
The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) National Flood Hazard Layer Viewer shows that the 
site is in an area of minimal flood hazard.  The flood hazard map is included in Appendix F. 
 
2.8 Surrounding Area Land Use 
 
The site is bordered by State Route 73 on the north, vacant, wooded land on the east, railroad tracks on 
the south, and agricultural fields on the west.  Agricultural land is located north of the site, across SR73 
and a golf course is located south of the site, across the railroad tracks.  Rombach Avenue is located 
approximately 1,600 feet south of the site.  Land use along Rombach Avenue is primarily commercial with 
some agricultural.  The nearest residential land use to the site is located approximately 2,000 feet north 
of the site. 
3.0 FIELD ACTIVITIES REVIEW 
 
3.1 Site Geology 
 
The 12 direct-push soil borings were advanced to terminal depths ranging from 12 to 31 feet bgs and were 
logged by a licensed professional geologist.  The boring logs and three cross-sections are included in 
Appendix A.  Bedrock was not encountered in any of the soil borings.  For clarity, all depths referred to in 
this section are below ground surface (bgs). 
 
The subsurface soil of the site consists primarily of clay and silty clay.  The clay was present down to depths 
ranging from 9 feet (B4 and B5) to 23.2 feet (B10).  Thin sand lenses of less than 0.3 feet in thickness were 
encountered at depths of 9 feet (B4), 14 feet (B9), and 11.5 feet (B10) and a 2-foot-thick layer of clayey 
sand was encountered at a depth of 9 feet (B5).  These sand lenses/layers were underlain by clay to depths 
ranging from 15.5 feet (B10) to 17 feet (B9).   
 
Well-graded gravel was encountered beneath the clay on the western side of the site, where the surface 
elevations are higher. The geologic maps reviewed indicated that this side of the site is covered with glacial 
end moraine deposits. Except for at B12, probe refusal occurred when this well-graded gravel layer was 
encountered. At B12, the well-graded gravel was underlain by clay. On the eastern side of the site, the 
clay was generally underlain by interbedded silt, sand, and clay.   
 
Groundwater was not encountered at B8 or B11.  Groundwater was encountered in the well-graded gravel 
at B1 (11.8 feet), B2 (12.8 feet) and B10 (15.5 feet).  Groundwater was encountered in sand at depths 
ranging from 13 feet to 17.8 feet at B3, B5, B6, B7, and B9 and was encountered in clay at a depth of 24 
feet at B12.

title: 1MP00060.pdf
text:
Soil and Site Evaluation  2065 Rombach Avenue 
Quasar Energy Group – Wilmington Nursery  Wilmington, Ohio 44177 
 
   
ENVi Environmental, LLC                                                                      - 7 - Elyria, Ohio 
 
 
Samples of the clay were collected in Shelby tubes at B4, B7, and B10 for permeability testing. The Shelby 
tubes are 3 inches in diameter and 30 inches long and are hydraulically pushed into the soil at the bottom 
of the open borehole to collect a relatively undist urbed soil sample.  Hollow-stem augers were used to 
drill boreholes next to the direct push boreholes to collect a Shelby tube sample at the desired depth.  The 
samples were obtained from depths of 12 to 14.5 feet (B4), 4 to 6.5 feet (B7), and 6 to 8.5 feet (B10).  The 
samples were delivered to the SME geotechnical test ing laboratory in Kirtland, Ohio for extrusion and 
permeability testing.   
The average permeability (k, coefficient of conductivity ) over the last 4 test cycles are provided in the 
following table: 
 
  
Sample Location Average Permeability (cm/s) 
B4, 12 – 14.5 feet 1.6 E-08 
B7, 4 – 6.5 feet 5.5 E-08 
B10, 6 – 8.5 feet 2.5 E-08 
 
The results are typical of clay soils, which genera lly have a permeability between E-07 and E-09.  The 
permeability testing data sheets are included in Appendix A. 
 
3.2 Site Soil Descriptions 
 
The soil at the 12 hand-augered test hole locations were logged and described by Jeff Rice, a Certified 
Professional Soil Scientist.  The Soil Descriptio n forms and a site map showing the soil units and 
topography of the site are included in Appendix B. 
 
The soil at test holes #1 through #7 and test holes # 10 and #11 was classified as the Fincastle soil series.  
The soil as test holes #8 and #9 was classified as th e Xenia soil series and the soil at test hole #12 was 
classified as the Russell soil series.  A perched seasonal water table was observed at depths ranging from 
5 inches (test hole 5) to 28 inches (test hole #8 and #11).   No perched seasonal water table was 
encountered at test hole #12.  No apparent water table, highly permeable material, or bedrock was 
e n c ou n t e r e d  a t  a n y of  t h e  t e s t  h ol e s .   N o r e s t r i c t i ve layers were observed at test holes #5, #7, or #9 
through #12.  Restrictive layers were observed at the other test holes at depths ranging from 23 inches 
(#1) to 54 inches (#3). 
 
4.0 CONCLUSIONS 
 
Based on the review of maps and geological resources and the results of the site-specific soil evaluation, 
the site is acceptable for beneficial use of Class B Biosolids to aid the growth of harvestable trees to be 
processed into mulch or bioenergy.   
 
The site meets the requirements of OAC 3745-42-13 (C)(2)(a) and (b), and (g) through (i)(v) as the following 
findings show:

acre.

Introduction 
Development of a Fact Sheet for NPDES permits is mandated by Title 40 of the Code of Federal Regulations, 
Section 124.8 and 124.56.  This document fulfills the requirements established in those regulations by providing 
the information necessary to inform the public of actions proposed by the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency, 
as well as the methods by which the public can participate in the process of finalizing those actions. 
 
This Fact Sheet is prepared in order to document the technical basis and risk management decisions that are 
considered in the determination of water quality based NPDES Permit effluent limitations.  The technical basis for 
the Fact Sheet may consist of evaluations of promulgated effluent guidelines, existing effluent quality, instream 
biological, chemical and physical conditions, and the relative risk of alternative effluent limitations.  This Fact 
Sheet details the discretionary decision-making process empowered to the Director by the Clean Water Act and 
Ohio Water Pollution Control Law (ORC 6111).  Decisions to award variances to Water Quality Standards or 
promulgated effluent guidelines for economic or technological reasons will also be justified in the Fact Sheet 
where necessary. 
 
No antidegradation review was necessary. 
 
Effluent limits based on available treatment technologies are required by Section 301(b) of the CWA.  Many of 
these have already been established by the United States Environmental Protection Agency (U.S. EPA) in the 
effluent guideline regulations (a.k.a. categorical regulations) for industry categories in 40 CFR Parts 405-499.  
Technology-based regulations for publicly owned treatment works are listed in the Secondary Treatment 
Regulations (40 CFR Part 133).  If regulations have not been established for a category of dischargers, the 
director may establish technology-based limits based on best professional judgment (BPJ). 
 
Ohio EPA reviews the need for water-quality-based limits on a pollutant-by-pollutant basis. Wasteload allocations 
(WLAs) are used to develop these limits based on the pollutants that have been detected in the discharge, and the

receiving water’s assimilative capacity.  The assimilative capacity depends on the flow in the water receiving the 
discharge, and the concentration of the pollutant upstream.  The greater the upstream flow, and the lower the 
upstream concentration, the greater the assimilative capacity is.  Assimilative capacity may represent dilution (as 
in allocations for metals), or it may also incorporate the break-down of pollutants in the receiving water (as in 
allocations for oxygen-demanding materials). 
 
The need for water-quality-based limits is determined by comparing the WLA for a pollutant to a measure of the 
effluent quality.  The measure of effluent quality is called Projected Effluent Quality (PEQ).  This is a statistical 
measure of the average and maximum effluent values for a pollutant.  As with any statistical method, the more 
data that exists for a given pollutant, the more likely that PEQ will match the actual observed data.  If there is a 
small data set for a given pollutant, the highest measured value is multiplied by a statistical factor to obtain a 
PEQ; for example, if only one sample exists, the factor is 6.2, for two samples - 3.8, for three samples - 3.0.  The 
factors continue to decline as samples sizes increase.  These factors are intended to account for effluent 
variability, but if the pollutant concentrations are fairly constant, these factors may make PEQ appear larger than 
it would be shown to be if more sample results existed. 
 
Procedures for Participation in the Formulation of Final Determinations

why the proposed modification should be changed, a request for a public meeting on the proposed modification 
and/or a request for notice of further actions concerning the modification.  All communications timely received 
will be considered in the final formulation of the modification.  If significant public interest is shown a public 
meeting will be held prior to finalization of the modification. 
 
Within thirty (30) days of the issuance of the proposed modification any officer of an agency of the state or of a 
political subdivision, acting in his representative capacity or any person aggrieved or adversely affected by 
issuance of it may request an adjudication hearing by submitting a written objection in accordance with Ohio 
Revised Code Section 3745.07.  Since all other conditions of the permit remain in effect, a hearing may not be 
requested on any issues other than the proposed modification.  If an adjudication hearing is requested, the existing 
NPDES permit will remain in effect until the hearing is resolved.  Following the finalization of the modification 
by the Director, any person who was a party to an adjudication hearing may appeal to the Environmental Review 
Appeals Commission. 
 
Requests for public meetings shall be in writing and shall state the action of the Director objected to, the questions

Citizens may conduct file reviews regarding specific companies or sites.  Appointments are necessary to conduct 
file reviews because requests to review files have increased dramatically in recent years. The first 250 pages 
copied are free. For requests to copy more than 250 pages, there is a five-cent charge for each page copied. 
Payment is required by check or money order, made payable to Treasurer State of Ohio. 
 
Location of Discharge/Receiving Water Use Classification 
The Wilmington wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) discharges to Lytle Creek at River Mile 6.83.  Figure 1 
shows the approximate location of the facility. 
 
This segment of Lytle Creek is described by Ohio EPA River Code: 11-212-000, Hydrologic Unit Code: 
05090202-06-03, County: Clinton, Ecoregion: Eastern Corn Belt Plains.  Lytle Creek is designated for the 
following uses under Ohio’s WQS (OAC 3745-1-18): Warmwater Habitat (WWH), General High Quality Water, 
Agricultural Water Supply, Industrial Water Supply, and Primary Contact Recreation. 
 
Use designations define the goals and expectations of a waterbody.  These goals are set for aquatic life protection, 
recreation use and water supply use, and are defined in the Ohio WQS (OAC 3745-1-07).  The use designations 
for individual waterbodies are listed in rules -08 through -32 of the Ohio WQS.  Once the goals are set, numeric 
WQS are developed to protect these uses.  Different uses have different water quality criteria. 
 
Use designations for aquatic life protection include habitats for coldwater fish and macroinvertebrates, warmwater 
aquatic life and waters with exceptional communities of warmwater organisms.  These uses all meet the goals of 
the federal CWA.  Ohio WQS also include aquatic life use designations for waterbodies which cannot meet the 
CWA goals because of human-caused conditions that cannot be remedied without causing fundamental changes 
to land use and widespread economic impact.  The dredging and clearing of some small streams to support 
agricultural or urban drainage is the most common of these conditions.  These streams are given Modified 
Warmwater or Limited Resource Water designations. 
 
Recreation uses are defined by the depth of the waterbody and the potential for wading or swimming.  Uses are 
defined for bathing waters, swimming/canoeing (Primary Contact Recreation) and wading only (Secondary 
Contact which are generally waters too shallow for swimming or canoeing). 
 
Water supply uses are defined by the actual or potential use of the waterbody.  Public Water Supply designations 
apply near existing water intakes so that waters are safe to drink with standard treatment.  Most other waters are 
designated for agricultural water supply and industrial water supply. 
 
FACILITY DESCRIPTION 
 
The Wilmington WWTP was constructed in 1936 and last upgraded in 1989.  The average design flow is 3.0 
million gallons per day (MGD), with a peak hydraulic capacity of 6.25 MGD.  Wilmington WWTP serves the city 
of Wilmington and the surrounding area. Wilmington WWTP has the following treatment processes which are 
shown on Figure 2:

 Screening 
 Grit removal 
 Primary clarification 
 Trickling filters

 Secondary clarification 
 Ultraviolet disinfection 
 
Wilmington WWTP has a secondary treatment bypass.  Flow bypasses the trickling filters, aerated contact tanks 
and secondary clarification and is combined with fully treated flow prior to disinfection.  In the NPDES permit, it 
is designated as station 1PD00013602 and has monitoring and reporting requirements.  Discharge through this 
station is prohibited except under emergency conditions as authorized by federal regulation at 40 CFR 122.41(m) 
and provisions in Part III of the permit.   
 
The city of Wilmington has 100% separate sanitary sewers in the collection system. 
 
The city of Wilmington has an approved pretreatment program. Two, categorical industrial users discharge 
approximately 0.11 MGD average daily flow into the sanitary sewer system.  Three significant, non-categorical 
industrial users discharge 0.24 MGD average daily flow as well. 
 
The City’s potable water comes from reservoirs. 
 
Wilmington WWTP utilizes the following sewage sludge treatment processes: 
 
 Gravity thickening 
 Sludge stabilization using aerobic digestion 
 
Treated sludge is either land applied at agronomic rates or disposed in a municipal landfill.   
 
Basis of the Modification 
The City of Wilmington has applied for a Permit to Install (PTI #1543170) to make improvements to their 
wastewater treatment plant and expand capacity from 3.0 to 4.5 MGD for average daily design flow.  The new 
peak hydraulic capacity will be 9.0 MGD and the bypass at station 602 will be eliminated.  The specific 
improvements involve replacement of the existing treatment plant with an influent pump station equipped with 
influent screens and grit removal, a four basin sequencing batch reactor, chemical feed system, tertiary disc 
filtration, ultraviolet radiation disinfection, and a cascade aerator (see figure 3).  A new sludge dewatering 
building for preparing sludge for disposal to a landfill is also included. The new plant effluent outfall will move  
approximately 1,100 feet east (upstream) of the existing outfall on Lytle Creek. 
 
Table 1 shows the proposed final limits for outfall 001.  The new limits are proposed to become effective on 
March 1, 2026, with the completion of the proposed facility expansion.  A schedule of compliance is included to 
meet the new final effluent limits discussed below.

Ammonia (summer), CBOD5, Dissolved Oxygen, and TSS 
The proposed limits for ammonia (summer), 5-day carbonaceous biochemical oxygen demand (CBOD5), 
dissolved oxygen, and total suspended solids (TSS) are technology based treatment standards included in OAC 
3745-1-05, Best Available Demonstrated Control Technology (BADCT).  The proposed loading limits are more 
restrictive than those in the current permit.  The summer ammonia limits required by BADCT were evaluated and 
determined to be protective of water quality standards for ammonia toxicity. 
 
Ammonia (winter) 
The proposed limits for ammonia (winter) are based on plant design associated with PTI 1543170.  The permittee 
has not requested an increase in load, therefore loading limits are proposed to remain the same as in the current 
permit but concentration limits are proposed to be lowered to account for the additional flow.  The proposed limits 
are more restrictive than BADCT and have been evaluated using the WLA procedure and determined to be 
protective of water quality standards for ammonia toxicity. 
 
Total Phosphorus 
The proposed limits for total phosphorus are based on plant design associated with PTI 1543170.  The permittee 
has not requested an increase in load, therefore loading limits are proposed to remain the same as in the current 
permit but concentration limits are proposed to be lowered to account for the additional flow. 
 
Additionally, a new seasonal loading limit is proposed based on best technical judgement for an adaptive 
management approach for implementation of the 2011 Total Maximum Daily load for the Lower Little Miami 
River report (TMDL).   The maximum limit is proposed to be applied to the average daily load for the critical 
season (June through October) and is proposed to be reported once per year in the October Discharge Monitoring 
Report.  The seasonal average daily load is proposed to be calculated according to this equation: 
 
Load = QM x CM x CF 
Where: 
 Q M = median daily flow rate (MGD) 
 C M = median total phosphorus effluent concentration 
 CF = unit conversion factor = 3.7854 
 
The TMDL is available on the Ohio EPA, Division of Surface Water website at: 
https://epa.ohio.gov/divisions-and-offices/surface-water/reports-data/little-miami-river-watershed 
 
Whole Effluent Toxicity 
A lower effluent limit for chronic whole effluent toxicity (WET) in Ceriodaphnia dubia is proposed to account 
for the additional flow. 
 
Other Requirements 
Monitoring for all other parameters required by the current permit is proposed to continue in the modified permit.  
A reasonable potential analysis showed that parameters other than those discussed above would not exceed the 
water quality standards for the receiving stream. 
 
A new station (1PD00013586) is proposed to be added for monitoring sludge disposal via hauling to a landfill. 
 
Compliance Schedule 
New Effluent Limits – a compliance schedule is proposed for the permittee to complete construction of the 
proposed facility expansion and attain compliance with the new effluent limits by March 1, 2026.  See Part I, C 
for details.

text:
Mike DeWine, Governor 
Jon Husted, Lt. Governor 
Anne M. Vogel, Director 
50 West Town Street • Suite 700 • P.O. Box 1049 • Columbus, OH 43216-1049 
epa.ohio.gov • (614) 644-3020 • (614) 644-3184 (fax) 
May 12, 2023 
Ohio EPA Permit No. 1PD00013*PD 
Application No. OH0028134 
Effective Date: July 1, 2023 
Facility Name:  City of Wilmington WWTP 
City of Wilmington  
Steven Honeycutt 
475 S Nelson Avenue 
Wilmington, OH 45177 
Dear Ladies and Gentlemen: 
In accordance with Rule 3745-33-04 (D) of the Ohio Administrative Code (formerly Ohio EPA Regulation 
EP-31-06), the above referenced NPDES Permit is hereby modified as follows: 
Revision 
1) Page 3, added Total Phosphorus loading (kg) monitoring.
2) Page 5, modified final effluent limits for Dissolved Oxygen to 6.0 mg/l minimum, Total
Suspended Solids to 18 mg/l weekly and 12 mg/l monthly with lowered loading limits, Ammonia
Nitrogen Summer limits to 1.5 mg/l weekly and 1.0 mg/l monthly, Ammonia Nitrogen Winter
limits to 2.35 mg/l weekly and 1.53 mg/l monthly, Total Phosphorus to 1.0 mg/l weekly and 0.67
mg/l monthly during the period June through October with monitoring only during the period
November through May.
3) Page 6, added Total Phosphorus loading limit of 8.5 kg calculated for the period June
through October.  Modified Chronic Toxicity, Ceriodaphnia dubia, limit to 1.08 TUc.
4) Page 7, modified CBOD 5 day final effluent limits to 15 mg/l weekly and 10 mg/l monthly
with lowered loading limits, modified effluent loadings based on average design flow of 4.5
MGD. Added note g. regarding total Phosphorus Loading Limit.
5) Page 12, added sludge monitoring station 586.
6) Page 20, added E. Municipal Wastewater Treatment Plant Construction Schedule to meet
Final Limits at Outfall 001.
7) Page 32, added Item AA. Total Phosphorus Loading Limitation.
All terms and conditions of the existing permit not recommended for modification by this document will 
remain in effect. Any modified term or condition contained in this modification shall supersede, on the 
date this modification is effective, the existing respective term or condition of the permit. 
When the modification is effective, the Ohio EPA permit number will be changed to 1PD00013*QD. The 
application number will remain OH0028134. Attached is a copy of the updated NPDES permit.   
Sincerely, 
Anne M. Vogel 
Director

NOTES for Station Number 1PD00013300:  
 
a. A sanitary sewer overflow is an overflow, spill, release, or diversion of wastewater from a sanitary sewer system. Although the above table indicates that the 
Measuring Frequency for Overflow Occurrence is 1/Month, the intent of that provision is to specify a reporting frequency for Overflow Occurrence, not a 
monitoring frequency. The monitoring requirement under this permit is that these overflows shall be monitored on each day when they discharge. Only sanitary 
sewer overflows that enter waters of the state, either directly or through a storm sewer or other conveyance, must be reported under this monitoring station.  
 
b. For the purpose of counting occurrences, each location on the sanitary sewer system where there is an overflow, spill, release, or diversion of wastewater on a 
given day that enters waters of the state is counted as one occurrence. For example, if on a given day overflows occur from a manhole at one location and from a 
damaged pipe at another location and they both enter waters of the state, record two occurrences for that day. If overflows from both locations continue on the 
following day, record two occurrences for the following day. At the end of the month, total the daily occurrences and report this number on Day 1 of the DMR. If 
there are no overflows during the entire month, report "zero" (0).  
 
c. All sanitary sewer overflows are prohibited.  
 
d. See Part II, Items D and E.

NOTES for Station Number 1PD00013581: 
 
a. Monitoring is required when sewage sludge is removed from the permittee's facility for application to the land. The monitoring data shall be reported on the 
December Discharge Monitoring Report (DMR). The monitoring data can be collected at any time during the reporting period.  
 
b. Metal analysis must be completed during each reporting period whether or not sewage sludge is removed from the facility and applied to the land. Alternatively, 
the number of composite samples collected and reported prior to the next land application event shall be increased to account for the reporting period(s) in which 
land application did not occur. If all accumulated sewage sludge has been removed and hauled to a landfill, incinerated or transferred to another NPDES permit 
holder, then the metal analysis is not required.  
 
c. If no sewage sludge is removed from the facility during the reporting period, enter the results for the metal analysis on the DMR and enter "0" for sludge weight 
and sludge fee weight.  
 
d. If no sewage sludge is removed from the facility during the reporting period and no metal analysis is completed during the reporting period, select the "No 
Discharge" check box on the data entry form and PIN the eDMR.  
 
e. If metal analysis has not been completed previously during each reporting period: when sewage sludge is removed from the facility all metal analysis results 
shall be reported on the applicable DMR by entering the separate results on different days within the DMR. For example, if no sewage sludge has been removed 
from the facility for a full calendar year, and quarterly monitoring is required by the permit, then five (four from the previous year and one for the current

B. Lower Little Miami River Total Maximum Daily Load (TMDL) Implementation Schedule 
 
The "Total Maximum Daily Loads for the Lower Little Miami River Watershed", approved by U.S EPA 
on March 28, 2011, established the following wasteload allocation for the Wilmington wastewater 
treatment plant: 
 
Total phosphorus - 0.913 kg/day, 0.08 mg/l at average daily design flow (3.0 MGD). 
 
The TMDL report also established an iterative, adaptive implementation approach. 
 
Consistent with the adaptive implementation approach, this compliance schedule provides time for 
making the initial phosphorus reduction, time for responses in ambient water quality and biological 
conditions to occur, and time to evaluate the response in the stream biology. The approach is repeated 
through a series of steps to achieve biological attainment in Lytle Creek.  
 
As soon as possible, but not later than the timeframes developed in accordance with the 
following schedule, the permittee shall reduce total phosphorus loads to the receiving stream until excess 
total phosphorus no longer limits the biological community from attaining applicable criteria or the waste 
load allocation in the TMDL is achieved at station number 1PD00013001. 
 
1. The permittee shall submit an annual status report to the Ohio EPA Southwest District Office that 
includes the monthly average total phosphorus effluent concentrations for the previous 12 months; a 
summary of any additional source reduction measures, operational improvements, or minor facility 
modifications taken to maximize the ability of existing treatment facilities to reduce discharges of total 
phosphorus; and a summary of other projects, initiatives or activities the permittee has taken to achieve 
loading reductions of total phosphorus. The first annual report shall be submitted by September 1, 
2022.  (Event Code 95999)  COMPLETED 
 
2. The city of Wilmington has substantially reduced the total phosphorus loading being discharged from 
the Wilmington wastewater treatment works since the Lytle Creek's attainment status was last evaluated. 
Ohio EPA recognizes that the receiving stream will need to be reassessed to evaluate the impact of total 
phosphorus reductions before further reductions are required.  
 
If a stream reassessment demonstrates Lytle Creek continues to be impaired by excessive total 
phosphorus loadings and the Wilmington wastewater treatment works causes or has the reasonable 
potential to cause or contributes to the impairment, the city of Wilmington shall submit a general plan for 
achieving the wasteload allocation of 0.913 kg/day for total phosphorus. This permit shall either be 
modified or renewed to establish the due date for the submittal of the general plan. The general plan shall 
include the actions to be taken by the City to achieve incremental load reductions for total phosphorus of 
2.614 kg/day and the amount of time required to achieve said reductions.  
 
If it is determined that load reductions for total phosphorus are required, the incremental load reduction of 
2.614 kg/day shall be included in a compliance schedule within the subsequent NPDES permit. Ohio EPA 
will reassess the receiving stream after each incremental load reduction has been achieved to determine 
the streams attainment status. The process of load reductions and stream reassessments shall continue 
until such time as either evidence becomes available demonstrating to the Director's satisfaction that the

D. Sanitary Sewer Overflow (SSO) Reporting Requirements  
 
A sanitary sewer overflow is an overflow, spill, release, or diversion of wastewater from a sanitary sewer 
system. SSOs do not include wet weather discharges from combined sewer overflows specifically listed 
in Part II of this NPDES permit (if any). All SSOs are prohibited. 
 
1. Reporting for SSOs That Imminently and Substantially Endanger Human Health 
 
a) Immediate Notification 
 
You must notify Ohio EPA (1-800-282-9378) and the appropriate Board of Health (i.e., city or county) 
within 24 hours of learning of any SSO from your sewers or from your maintenance contract areas that

1PD00013*QD 
 
may imminently and substantially endanger human health. The telephone report must identify the 
location, estimated volume and receiving water, if any, of the overflow. An SSO that may imminently and 
substantially endanger human health includes dry weather overflows, major line breaks, overflow events 
that result in fish kills or other significant harm, overflows that expose the general public to contact with 
raw sewage, and overflow events that occur in sensitive waters and high exposure areas such as protection 
areas for public drinking water intakes and waters where primary contact recreation occurs. 
 
b) Follow-Up Written Report 
 
Within 5 days of the time you become aware of any SSO that may imminently and substantially endanger 
human health, you must provide the appropriate Ohio EPA district office a written report that includes: 
 
(i) the estimated date and time when the overflow began and stopped or will be stopped  
 (if known); 
(ii) the location of the SSO including an identification number or designation if one exists; 
(iii) the receiving water (if there is one); 
(iv) an estimate of the volume of the SSO (if known);  
(v) a description of the sewer system component from which the release occurred (e.g., manhole, 
constructed overflow pipe, crack in pipe); 
(vi) the cause or suspected cause of the overflow; 
(vii) steps taken or planned to reduce, eliminate, and prevent reoccurrence of the  
 overflow and a schedule of major milestones for those steps; and  
(viii) steps taken or planned to mitigate the impact(s) of the overflow and a schedule 
 of major milestones for those steps. 
 
An acceptable 5-day follow-up written report can be filled-in or downloaded from the Ohio EPA Division 
of Surface Water Permits Program Technical Assistance Web page at 
http://www.epa.ohio.gov/dsw/permits/technical_assistance.aspx . 
 
2. Reporting for All SSOs, Including Those That Imminently and Substantially Endanger Human Health  
 
a) Discharge Monitoring Reports (DMR)  
 
Sanitary sewer overflows that enter waters of the state, either directly or through a storm sewer or other 
conveyance, shall be reported on your Discharge Monitoring Reports (DMR). You must report the 
system-wide number of occurrences for SSOs that enter waters of the state in accordance with the 
requirements for station number 300. A monitoring table for this station is included in Part I, B of this 
NPDES permit.  
 
For the purpose of counting occurrences, each location on the sanitary sewer system where there is an 
overflow, spill, release, or diversion of wastewater on a given day is counted as one occurrence. For 
example, if on a given day overflows occur from a manhole at one location and from a damaged pipe at 
another location and they both enter waters of the state, you should record two occurrences for that day. If 
overflows from both locations continue on the following day, you should record two occurrences for the 
following day. At the end of the month, total the daily occurrences from all locations on your system and 
report this number using reporting code 74062 (Overflow Occurrence, No./Month) on the 4500 form for 
station number 300.  
 
b) Annual Report  
 
You must prepare an annual report of all SSOs in your collection system, including those that do not enter

Y. Pretreatment Program Requirements 
 
The permittee's pretreatment program initially approved on December 14, 1984, and all subsequent 
modifications approved before the effective date of this permit, shall be an enforceable term and condition 
of this permit. 
 
1. Legal Authority  
 
The permittee shall adopt and maintain legal authority which enables it to fully implement and enforce all 
aspects of its approved pretreatment program including the identification and characterization of 
industrial sources, issuance of control documents, compliance monitoring and reporting, and enforcement. 
The permittee shall establish agreements with all contributing jurisdictions, as necessary, to enable the 
permittee to fulfill its requirements with respect to industrial users discharging to its system.  
 
2. Funding 
 
The permittee shall have sufficient resources and qualified personnel to fully implement all aspects of its 
approved pretreatment program. 
 
3. Industrial User Inventory  
 
The permittee shall identify all industrial users subject to pretreatment standards and requirements and 
characterize the nature and volume of pollutants in their wastewater. Dischargers determined to be 
Significant Industrial Users according to OAC 3745-3-01 must be notified of applicable pretreatment 
standards and requirements within 30 days of making such a determination. This inventory shall be 
updated at a frequency to ensure proper identification and characterization of industrial users.

least once during the term of each significant industrial user's control mechanism. Existing significant 
industrial users shall be evaluated within one year of the effective date of this permit if the users have 
never been evaluated. New industrial users identified as significant industrial users shall be evaluated 
within one year of being identified as a significant industrial user.

pollutants into the POTW which will interfere with the operation of the POTW, pass through the

Part III - GENERAL CONDITIONS 
 
1. DEFINITIONS  
 
"Daily discharge" means the discharge of a pollutant measured during a calendar day or any 24-hour 
period that reasonably represents the calendar day for purposes of sampling. For pollutants with 
limitations expressed in units of mass, the "daily discharge" is calculated as the total mass of the pollutant 
discharged over the day. For pollutants with limitations expressed in other units of measurement, the 
"daily discharge" is calculated as the average measurement of the pollutant over the day.  
 
"Average weekly" discharge limitation means the highest allowable average of "daily discharges'' over a 
calendar week, calculated as the sum of all "daily discharges'' measured during a calendar week divided 
by the number of "daily discharges'' measured during that week. Each of the following 7-day periods is 
defined as a calendar week: Week 1 is Days 1 - 7 of the month; Week 2 is Days 8 - 14; Week 3 is Days 15 
- 21; and Week 4 is Days 22 - 28. If the "daily discharge" on days 29, 30 or 31 exceeds the "average 
weekly" discharge limitation, Ohio EPA may elect to evaluate the last 7 days of the month as Week 4 
instead of Days 22 - 28. Compliance with fecal coliform bacteria or E coli bacteria limitations shall be 
determined using the geometric mean.  
 
"Average monthly" discharge limitation means the highest allowable average of "daily discharges" over a 
calendar month, calculated as the sum of all "daily discharges" measured during a calendar month divided 
by the number of "daily discharges" measured during that month. Compliance with fecal coliform 
bacteria or E coli bacteria limitations shall be determined using the geometric mean. 
 
"85 percent removal" means the arithmetic mean of the values for effluent samples collected in a period 
of 30 consecutive days shall not exceed 15 percent of the arithmetic mean of the values for influent 
samples collected at approximately the same times during the same period.  
 
"Absolute Limitations" Compliance with limitations having descriptions of "shall not be less than," "nor 
greater than," "shall not exceed," "minimum," or "maximum" shall be determined from any single value 
for effluent samples and/or measurements collected.  
 
"Net concentration" shall mean the difference between the concentration of a given substance in a sample 
taken of the discharge and the concentration of the same substances in a sample taken at the intake which 
supplies water to the given process. For the purpose of this definition, samples that are taken to determine 
the net concentration shall always be 24-hour composite samples made up of at least six increments taken 
at regular intervals throughout the plant day.  
 
"Net Load" shall mean the difference between the load of a given substance as calculated from a sample 
taken of the discharge and the load of the same substance in a sample taken at the intake which supplies 
water to given process. For purposes of this definition, samples that are taken to determine the net loading 
shall always be 24-hour composite samples made up of at least six increments taken at regular intervals 
throughout the plant day.  
 
"MGD" means million gallons per day.  
 
"mg/l" means milligrams per liter.  
 
"ug/l" means micrograms per liter.  
 
"ng/l" means nanograms per liter.

2. GENERAL EFFLUENT LIMITATION 
 
The effluent shall, at all times, be free of substances:  
 
A. In amounts that will settle to form putrescent, or otherwise objectionable, sludge deposits; or that will 
adversely affect aquatic life or waterfowl;  
 
B. Of an oily, greasy, or surface-active nature, and of other floating debris, in amounts that will form 
noticeable accumulations of scum, foam, or sheen; 
 
C. In amounts that will alter the natural color or odor of the receiving water to such degree as to create a 
nuisance;  
 
D. In amounts that either singly or in combination with other substances are toxic to human, animal, or 
aquatic life;  
 
E. In amounts that are conducive to the growth of aquatic weeks or algae to the extent that such growth 
become inimical to more desirable forms of aquatic life, or create conditions that are unsightly, or 
constitute a nuisance in any other fashion;  
 
F. In amounts that will impair designated instream or downstream water uses

compliance with the terms and conditions of this permit. Proper operation and maintenance also includes

operation of back-up or auxiliary facilities or similar systems which are installed by a permittee only 
when the operation is necessary to achieve compliance with conditions of the permit.  
 
B. The permittee shall effectively monitor the operation and efficiency of treatment and control facilities 
and the quantity and quality of the treated discharge.

Part IV.  Stormwater Control Measures and Pollution Prevention Programs 
In Part IV and in Part VI, the term “minimize” means reduce and/or eliminate to the extent achievable using 
control measures (including best management practices) that are technologically available and 
economically practicable and achievable in light of best industry practice. 
A. Control Measures. 
You shall select, design, install, and implement control measures (including best management 
practices) to address the selection and design considerations in Part IV.B, and meet the control 
measures/best management practices in Part IV.C and any applicable numeric effluent limits in Part I.  
The selection, design, installation, and implementation of these control measures shall be in accordance 
with good engineering practices and manufacturer’s specifications.  Note that you may deviate from 
such manufacturer’s specifications where you provide justification for such deviation and include 
documentation of your rationale in the part of your SWPPP that describes your control measures, 
consistent with Part IV.J.3.  If you find that your control measures are not achieving their intended 
effect of minimizing pollutant discharges, you shall modify these control measures as expeditiously as 
practicable.  Regulated stormwater discharges from your facility include stormwater run-on that 
commingles with stormwater discharges associated with industrial activity at your facility. 
B. Control Measure Selection and Design Considerations. 
You shall consider the following when selecting and designing control measures: 
1. Preventing stormwater from coming into contact with polluting materials is generally more 
effective, and less costly, than trying to remove pollutants from stormwater; 
2. Using control measures in combination is more effective than using control measures in isolation 
for minimizing pollutants in your stormwater discharge;   
3. Assessing the type and quantity of pollutants, including their potential to impact receiving water 
quality, is critical to designing effective control measures that will achieve the limits in this permit; 
4. Minimizing impervious areas at your facility and infiltrating runoff onsite (including bioretention 
cells, green roofs, and pervious pavement, among other approaches) can reduce runoff and improve 
groundwater recharge and stream base flows in local streams, although care shall be taken to avoid 
ground water contamination; 
5. Attenuating flow using open vegetated swales and natural depressions can reduce in-stream impacts 
of erosive flows; 
6. Conserving and/or restoring of riparian buffers will help protect streams from stormwater runoff 
and improve water quality; and 
7. Using treatment interceptors (e.g., swirl separators and sand filters) may be appropriate in some 
instances to minimize the discharge of pollutants.

C. Control Measures/Best Management Practices (BMPs) 
1. Minimize Exposure.  You shall minimize the exposure of manufacturing, processing, and material 
storage areas (including loading and unloading, storage, disposal, cleaning, maintenance, and 
fueling operations) to rain, snow, snowmelt, and runoff by either locating these industrial materials 
and activities inside or protecting them with storm resistant coverings (although significant 
enlargement of impervious surface area is not recommended).  In minimizing exposure, you should 
pay particular attention to the following: 
a. Use grading, berming, or curbing to prevent runoff of contaminated flows and divert run-on 
away from these areas; 
b. Locate materials, equipment, and activities so that leaks are contained in existing containment 
and diversion systems (confine the storage of leaky or leak-prone vehicles and equipment 
awaiting maintenance to protected areas); 
c. Clean up spills and leaks promptly using dry methods (e.g., absorbents) to prevent the discharge 
of pollutants; 
d. Use drip pans and absorbents under or around leaky vehicles and equipment or store indoors 
where feasible;  
e. Use spill/overflow protection equipment; 
f. Drain fluids from equipment and vehicles prior to on-site storage or disposal; 
g. Perform all cleaning operations indoors, under cover, or in bermed areas that prevent runoff 
and run-on and also that capture any overspray; and 
h. Ensure that all washwater drains to a proper collection system (i.e., not the stormwater drainage 
system). 
If the discharge of vehicle and equipment washwater is not authorized under Part I of this permit, 
these wastewaters must be discharged to sanitary sewer in accordance with applicable industrial 
pretreatment requirements or disposed of otherwise in accordance with applicable law. 
Note: Industrial materials do not need to be enclosed or covered if stormwater runoff from affected 
areas will not be discharged to receiving waters or if discharges are authorized under Part I of this 
permit. 
2. Good Housekeeping.  You shall keep clean all exposed areas that are potential sources of pollutants, 
using such measures as sweeping at regular intervals, keeping materials orderly and labeled, and 
storing materials in appropriate containers. 
3. Maintenance.  You shall regularly inspect, test, maintain, and repair all industrial equipment and 
systems to avoid situations that may result in leaks, spills, and other releases of pollutants in

stormwater discharged to receiving waters.  You shall maintain all control measures that are used 
to achieve the control measures/best management practices (BMPs) required by this permit in 
effective operating condition.  Nonstructural control measures shall also be diligently maintained 
(e.g., spill response supplies available, personnel appropriately trained).  If you find that your 
control measures need to be replaced or repaired, you shall make the necessary repairs or 
modifications as expeditiously as practicable.   
4. Spill Prevention and Response Procedures.  You shall minimize the potential for leaks, spills and 
other releases that may be exposed to stormwater and develop plans for effective response to such 
spills if or when they occur.  At a minimum, you shall implement: 
a. Procedures for plainly labeling containers (e.g., “Used Oil,” “Spent Solvents,” “Fertilizers and 
Pesticides,” etc.) that could be susceptible to spillage or leakage to encourage proper handling 
and facilitate rapid response if spills or leaks occur; 
b. Preventative measures such as barriers between material storage and traffic areas, secondary 
containment provisions, and procedures for material storage and handling; 
c. Procedures for expeditiously stopping, containing, and cleaning up leaks, spills, and other 
releases.  Employees who may cause, detect, or respond to a spill or leak shall be trained in 
these procedures and have necessary spill response equipment available.  If possible, one of 
these individuals should be a member of your stormwater pollution prevention team (Part 
IV.J.1); and 
d. Procedures for notification of appropriate facility personnel, emergency response agencies, and 
regulatory agencies. Where a leak, spill or other release containing a hazardous substance or 
oil in an amount equal to or in excess of a reportable quantity established under either 40 CFR 
Part 110, 40 CFR Part 117, or 40 CFR Part 302, occurs during a 24-hour period, you shall 
notify the Ohio EPA in accordance with the requirements of Part III Item 12 of this permit as 
soon as you have knowledge of the discharge. Contact information shall be in locations that 
are readily accessible and available. 
5. Erosion and Sediment Controls.  You shall stabilize exposed areas and contain runoff using 
structural and/or non-structural control measures to minimize onsite erosion and sedimentation, 
and the resulting discharge of pollutants.  Among other actions you shall take to meet this limit, 
you shall place flow velocity dissipation devices at discharge locations and within outfall channels 
where necessary to reduce erosion and/or settle out pollutants. In selecting, designing, installing, 
and implementing appropriate control measures, you are encouraged to consult with the current 
edition of Ohio’s Rainwater and Land Development manual (https://epa.ohio.gov/divisions-and-
